###### Abstract

Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly improved through
interaction rather than static supervision. Yet most self-evolution
methods adapt either the policy or the learning environment in
isolation, leaving a structural gap: as the agent’s capability frontier
shifts during training, the environment that provides supervision often
remains static or only weakly coupled to the agent’s revealed failures.
We call this mismatch _Agent-Environment Misalignment_. We propose SEAL,
a closed-loop co-evolution framework for interactive tool-use agents.
SEAL collects on-policy trajectories under executable verification,
diagnoses failed rollouts into turn-level labels, and uses these
diagnoses as a shared signal for both environment-side adaptation and
model-side policy optimization. Specifically, the training-time learning
interface evolves to expose clearer tool affordance cues, constraint
information, and recovery-oriented feedback, while the policy is updated
with diagnosis-guided advantage reweighting. Across in-distribution and
out-of-distribution multi-turn tool-use evaluations, SEAL consistently
improves low-resource agent learning: with only 400 training samples, it
yields +8.25 to +26.25 average-point gains across three backbones and
exhibits positive out-of-distribution transfer. These results show that
jointly adapting the learner and its training-time learning substrate is
a practical path toward more robust self-improving LLM agents.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have recently demonstrated strong
capabilities in reasoning, planning, and tool use, enabling progress on
interactive tasks that require multi-step decision making, multimodal
reasoning, and external action execution ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib1);
[Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib10); [Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib2);
[Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib44); [Yu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib45)). Recent
work further improves these agents through reinforcement learning,
tool-use post-training, agentic data generation, and multimodal data
evolution ([Qian et al., 2025](#bib.bib34); [Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib36); [Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib47)). A growing trend behind these advances is
_self-evolution through interaction_: agents improve by collecting
rollout trajectories, receiving feedback, and iteratively refining their
behavior through reflection, reinforcement learning, self-generated
supervision, or visual skill memory ([Wang et al., 2023a](#bib.bib13);
[Zhai et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib37); [Sun et
al., 2025](#bib.bib38); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). This paradigm
turns interaction feedback into a reusable source of supervision,
offering a scalable path beyond static offline training.

#### Practical motivation.

This promise becomes especially important in realistic tool-use
settings, where agents must operate through multi-turn interfaces,
satisfy strict execution constraints, and recover from partial failures
([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Xie et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Liu et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib31); [Yin and Du, 2026](#bib.bib32); [Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33); [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)). In such
environments, improvement depends not only on how the policy is
optimized, but also on what learning signals the training-time
environment exposes while the policy is changing. Yet current
self-evolving agents often adapt only one side of this interaction loop.

#### Two one-sided adaptation patterns.

Most existing methods follow one of two paths. (i) Model-centric
evolution. These methods improve the policy through rollout replay,
self-reflection, reward optimization, or post-training updates ([Huang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Yuan et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Wang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Xiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). While
effective, they typically optimize the agent against a largely fixed
learning environment, making the learning signal dependent on the
current policy’s own rollout distribution. In long-horizon interactive
settings with sparse rewards, this self-referential rollout distribution
can lead to policy-induced exploration bias, unstable recovery, and
inefficient credit assignment ([Shridhar et al., 2020](#bib.bib12)).
(ii) Environment-centric evolution. These methods adapt curricula, task
distributions, synthetic instructions, or interaction experiences. They
recognize that agent capability is shaped not only by optimization, but
also by the experiences exposed during training. Yet when such
adaptation is not grounded in the current agent’s executable
failures—what it can solve, where it repeatedly fails, and why—the
evolved environment may remain weakly coupled to the learner’s actual
needs. Such methods can increase diversity or difficulty, but without
executable failure grounding, they may still fail to target the
capability gaps that currently limit agent performance ([Bengio et al.,
2009](#bib.bib30); [Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib40); [Yang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib41); [Hao et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)).

#### A shared closed-loop bottleneck.

These two adaptation patterns look different, but they expose the same
structural problem: the training-time learning environment fails to
track the agent’s evolving capability boundary, and therefore provides
signals that are too static, weakly targeted, or insufficiently
informative. We refer to this mismatch as Agent-Environment
Misalignment. Importantly, by “environment” we refer to the
training-time learning substrate—including task exposure, observation
interfaces, action constraints, and recovery feedback—rather than
changes to the evaluation benchmark, tool semantics, or executable
verifier.

A concrete example illustrates the issue. When a tool call fails because
the agent uses a city name where an airport code is required, a fixed
environment may only return a generic execution error. Such feedback
tells the agent that the trajectory failed, but not whether the failure
came from missing a prerequisite lookup, using an invalid argument type,
or failing to recover after the error. As a result, the policy receives
only weak diagnostic supervision, and future trajectories are collected
under similarly uninformative conditions.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of self-evolution paradigms for LLM
agents. SEAL closes the loop between policy learning and environment

#### Our approach.

Motivated by this observation, we propose SEAL, a closed-loop
co-evolution framework for interactive tool-use agents. SEAL uses
verifier-grounded failure diagnoses as a shared signal for both sides of
training: it evolves the training-time interface with schema cues,
constraint information, and recovery-oriented feedback, and it reweights
policy-gradient updates by diagnostic utility. This enables
_capability-aware_ environment adaptation: instead of relying on generic
difficulty scaling or unguided data expansion, the training interface is
adjusted according to the current policy’s recurring failures, producing
more informative rollouts while leaving the benchmark protocol
unchanged. Extensive experiments on low-resource multi-turn tool-use
settings validate the effectiveness of this design. Our contributions
are threefold:

- •
  We identify Agent-Environment Misalignment: as the agent’s capability
  frontier shifts during training, the learning environment often
  remains static or only weakly coupled to the agent’s revealed
  failures.
- •
  We introduce SEAL, which uses verifier-grounded failure diagnosis to
  jointly evolve the training-time learning interface and guide policy
  optimization.
- •
  We show that SEAL improves low-resource multi-turn tool-use learning,
  yielding up to +26.25 average-point gains across three backbones with
  only 400 training samples and demonstrating positive transfer to
  held-out settings.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Model-Side Self-Improvement

Prior work shows that LLM agents can improve through repeated
interaction rather than static prompting alone. Methods based on
recursive skill learning, self-consolidation, reflective prompt
adaptation, memory-based improvement, and reinforcement learning from
interaction feedback primarily refine the agent itself ([Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17); [Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18); [Agrawal et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28); [Zweiger et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)). In this sense,
they are largely _model-centric_: experience is internalized into the
policy, prompt, memory, or skill library, while the training-time
learning environment is typically kept fixed. SEAL is complementary: it
uses failed trajectories not only for model-side improvement, but also
as verifier-grounded evidence for adapting the environment from which
future trajectories are collected.

### 2.2 Environment-Side Adaptation

Another line of work adapts what the learner is exposed to during
training. Curriculum learning, automatic curriculum design, synthetic
instruction generation, task evolution, and tool or skill construction
reshape the training distribution or interface ([Matiisen et al.,
2020](#bib.bib3); [Portelas et al., 2020](#bib.bib4); [Wang et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib5); [Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Cai et al.,
2023](#bib.bib22); [Qian et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Yuan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)). However, most such methods operate at the level of
task diversity, difficulty, or coverage. By contrast, SEAL performs
_failure-conditioned_ environment adaptation: verifier-grounded
diagnoses determine which affordance cues, constraint information,
recovery feedback, and training-time signals are exposed to target the
current policy’s capability gaps.

### 2.3 Interactive Environments and Co-Evolution

Interactive benchmarks for tool use, function calling, web navigation,
operating-system control, embodied simulation, and software engineering
expose the multi-turn dependencies, execution constraints, sparse
rewards, and recovery dynamics central to realistic agent learning
([Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Zhou
et al., 2023](#bib.bib8); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib11); [Jimenez et
al., 2023](#bib.bib9)). Recent work also studies environment design and
agent–environment co-evolution ([Xi et al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Zhang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). SEAL is closest
to this perspective, but under a stricter protocol: it keeps benchmark
tasks, tool semantics, and the executable verifier fixed, and adapts
only the training-time learning interface in a failure-conditioned,
verifier-grounded way.

## 3 Methodology

We propose SEAL, a framework for co-evolving tool-use policies and their
training-time learning environments. Key idea. Instead of treating the
environment as a fixed executor that returns only sparse scalar rewards,
SEAL exposes a verifier-grounded diagnostic interface during training,
converting failed interactions into structured evidence about the
agent’s current capability gaps while preserving tool semantics, task
labels, rewards, and the evaluation verifier.

Scope of adaptation. Here, the “environment” includes not only the
executable tool backend but also the learning interface through which
the policy observes tool schemas, execution feedback, and recovery
signals. SEAL therefore restricts environment evolution to this
interface layer to preserve benchmark fairness. The same diagnoses drive
both sides of the learning loop: they adapt the training-time interface
through tool affordance cues, recovery-oriented feedback, and
capability-specific hints, and they modulate policy optimization through
diagnosis-guided advantage reweighting. Figure
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
summarizes this co-evolution process.

![Refer to caption](2605.24426v1/image-2.png)

Figure 2: SEAL training-time co-evolution loop. The agent interacts with
an executable tool environment to produce multi-turn trajectories, which
are diagnosed into verifier-grounded failure types. These diagnoses
jointly drive learning-interface evolution through adapted training
observations and policy optimization through diagnosis-guided trajectory
weighting, while keeping tool semantics and evaluation fixed.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

We formulate interactive tool use as a partially observable decision
process:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{T},O_{\mathcal{E}},H,\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{goal}}\rangle,
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{S}`$ is the hidden state space, $`\mathcal{A}`$ is the
action space, $`\mathcal{O}`$ is the observation space, $`\mathcal{T}`$
is the transition function, $`O_{\mathcal{E}}`$ is the observation
function, $`H`$ is the horizon, and $`\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{goal}}`$
denotes goal states. In tool-use environments, actions include
natural-language responses and executable tool calls over a tool set
$`\mathcal{F}`$, while observations include dialogue context, tool
outputs, and execution errors.

Given an instruction $`q\sim\mathcal{D}`$, a policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$
interacts with an executable environment $`\mathcal{E}`$ and induces a
rollout

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau=\{(u_{i},a_{i},o_{i})\}_{i=1}^{T}\sim P_{\mathcal{E}}(\cdot\mid q,\pi_{\theta}),\qquad T\leq H,
``` |  | (2) |

where $`u_{i}`$ denotes the dialogue context, $`a_{i}`$ is the model
action, and $`o_{i}`$ is the environment observation. The executable
verifier $`\mathcal{V}`$ provides a terminal binary reward:

|     |                                                    |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(\tau,q,\mathcal{E})\in\{0,1\}.
       ```                                                 |     | (3) |

Standard RL maximizes the expected verifier success:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\pi_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D},\,\tau\sim P_{\mathcal{E}}(\cdot\mid q,\pi_{\theta})}[r(\tau)].
``` |  | (4) |

This scalar reward indicates whether a trajectory succeeds, but not why
it fails. SEAL therefore augments the training-time feedback as
$`(r(\tau),Z(\tau))`$, where $`Z(\tau)`$ denotes structured failure
diagnoses extracted from executable interaction traces. The verifier
reward, tool semantics, and evaluation protocol remain unchanged.

### 3.2 Verifier-Grounded Failure Diagnosis

For each rollout $`\tau`$, SEAL produces turn-level diagnostic labels

|     |                                                            |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       Z(\tau)=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}\},\qquad z_{i}\in\mathcal{Z},
       ```                                                         |     | (5) |

where each $`z_{i}`$ denotes the dominant outcome or failure mode at
turn $`i`$. Diagnoses are grounded in executable evidence rather than
free-form model critique: SEAL uses parser checks, tool-schema
validation, execution errors, observable state transitions, and verifier
comparisons to identify invalid or missing tool calls, argument or state
mismatches, recovery failures, and final-response mismatches.

We write the diagnosis function as

|     |                                                      |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       z_{i}=\Psi(a_{i},\xi_{i},s_{i-1},s_{i},\mathcal{F}),
       ```                                                   |     | (6) |

where $`a_{i}`$ is the model action, $`\xi_{i}`$ is the executable
evidence available at turn $`i`$, $`s_{i-1}`$ and $`s_{i}`$ are the pre-
and post-action states when available, and $`\mathcal{F}`$ is the
available tool set. Operationally, $`\Psi`$ is a deterministic
rule-based classifier over executable traces that prioritizes directly
executable failures over downstream verifier-level failures. The full
label taxonomy and decision rules are provided in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments").

Importantly, diagnosis does not modify the benchmark reward:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r(\tau)=\mathcal{V}(\tau,q,\mathcal{E}),\qquad Z(\tau)=\Psi(\tau,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{V}).
``` |  | (7) |

Thus, failed trajectories still receive zero reward under the original
verifier; the labels only add training-time structure for interface
evolution and policy optimization.

### 3.3 Learning-Interface Evolution

SEAL evolves only the *training-time learning interface*, not the
benchmark verifier, tool signatures, tool outputs, or task labels. Let
$`o_{i}`$ denote the original observation at turn $`i`$. SEAL constructs
an augmented training-time observation

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{o}_{i}=\Omega_{t}\left(o_{i},\mathcal{F},H_{t},C_{t}\right),
``` |  | (8) |

where $`\mathcal{F}`$ is the available tool set, $`H_{t}`$ is diagnostic
context accumulated from previous rollouts, and $`C_{t}`$ is the current
policy’s aggregate failure profile computed from recent diagnoses. The
transformation $`\Omega_{t}`$ changes only how existing environment
information is exposed to the learner.

In our implementation, $`\Omega_{t}`$ consists of three lightweight
components:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Omega_{t}(o_{i},\mathcal{F},H_{t},C_{t})=o_{i}\oplus\phi_{\mathrm{schema}}(\mathcal{F})\oplus\phi_{\mathrm{err}}(o_{i},H_{t})\oplus\phi_{\mathrm{cap}}(C_{t}).
``` |  | (9) |

Here, $`\phi_{\mathrm{schema}}`$ exposes schema-implied tool affordances
such as required arguments, enum constraints, argument types, and valid
tool-call formats. $`\phi_{\mathrm{err}}`$ converts execution errors
into recovery-oriented feedback without revealing the correct answer.
$`\phi_{\mathrm{cap}}`$ selects capability-specific cues from the
current failure profile so that recurring errors receive targeted
feedback.

The interface update is selected by failure type rather than benchmark
instance. For example, argument_mismatch activates schema and constraint
cues, missing_tool_call activates tool-affordance cues, and
recovery_failure activates structured error feedback. These cues clarify
how to repair an error class without exposing the reference tool
sequence, hidden parameters, or final answer. Throughout training, SEAL
preserves the original tool semantics and verifier; at evaluation time,
the evolved interface is removed.

### 3.4 Diagnosis-Guided Advantage Reweighting

Sparse verifier rewards indicate whether a trajectory succeeds, but not
how useful it is for policy improvement. In multi-turn tool use, two
failed trajectories with the same zero reward can have very different
learning value: invalid arguments or missed tool calls usually provide
clearer corrective signals than failures that appear only in the final
response. SEAL therefore uses verifier-grounded diagnoses to estimate
the *learning utility* of each trajectory and allocate optimization
pressure accordingly.

For a trajectory $`\tau_{j}`$, we first summarize its turn-level
diagnostic labels into an empirical diagnostic profile:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{j}(z)=\frac{1}{T_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{T_{j}}\mathbf{1}[z_{i}=z],\qquad z\in\mathcal{Z}.
``` |  | (10) |

This profile captures the dominant failure modes in the trajectory. We
then define a diagnostic utility function
$`\rho:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}`$, where $`\rho(z)`$
measures how actionable and attributable diagnosis type $`z`$ is.
Failures with concrete executable evidence and clear repair directions,
such as invalid_tool_call or argument_mismatch, receive larger utility,
while more ambiguous failures such as response_mismatch receive smaller
utility. In our experiments, $`\rho(z)`$ is fixed across all backbones
and training runs; exact values are reported in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments").

The trajectory-level diagnostic weight is computed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{j}=\operatorname{clip}\left(\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{j}(z)\rho(z),w_{\min},w_{\max}\right),
``` |  | (11) |

where clipping prevents rare or noisy diagnostic patterns from inducing
overly large policy updates. Given the original group-relative GRPO
advantage $`A_{j}`$, SEAL forms a diagnosis-weighted advantage:

|     |                               |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{A}_{j}=w_{j}A_{j}.
       ```                            |     | (12) |

This reweighting is a verifier-grounded preconditioning of the
policy-gradient signal. The verifier reward still determines the
direction through $`A_{j}`$, while the diagnostic utility scales how
much each trajectory contributes. Since $`w_{j}>0`$, the sign of the
advantage is unchanged, so SEAL does not alter the benchmark reward,
success criterion, or verifier-induced ranking; it simply prioritizes
trajectories whose failures are more attributable, recoverable, and
informative.

### 3.5 SEAL Training Loop

SEAL alternates between rollout collection, failure diagnosis, interface
evolution, and policy optimization. At round $`t`$, prompts are sampled
from the training distribution, and the current policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{t}}`$ interacts with the environment instantiated with
interface $`\Omega_{t}`$ to collect trajectories:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\{\tau_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}\sim P_{\mathcal{E}_{\Omega_{t}}}(\cdot\mid\pi_{\theta_{t}}).
``` |  | (13) |

Each trajectory is evaluated by the original verifier to obtain
$`r(\tau_{j})`$ and diagnosed to obtain $`Z(\tau_{j})`$. The diagnoses
are aggregated into a policy-specific failure profile:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{t}=\operatorname{Agg}\left(\{Z(\tau_{j})\}_{j=1}^{N}\right).
``` |  | (14) |

The failure profile updates the training-time interface:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Omega_{t+1}=\operatorname{Evolve}\left(\Omega_{t},C_{t}\right),
``` |  | (15) |

and the policy is optimized with diagnosis-weighted GRPO:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{t+1}=\operatorname{GRPO}\left(\theta_{t};\{\tau_{j},r(\tau_{j}),\widetilde{A}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}\right),\qquad\widetilde{A}_{j}=w_{j}A_{j}.
``` |  | (16) |

This forms a closed co-evolution loop between the policy and the
training-time learning interface: the agent reveals capability gaps, the
interface adapts around these gaps, and the model internalizes the
resulting feedback through policy optimization. Throughout the loop,
tool semantics, task labels, transition dynamics, rewards, and the
evaluation verifier remain fixed.

## 4 Experiments

We organize the evaluation around four questions: *What is the
experimental setup?* *How much does SEAL improve in-distribution
performance on BFCL V3?* *Do these gains transfer to held-out tool-use
settings?* and *Which components matter most, and how do the gains
emerge during training?*

### 4.1 Experiment Settings

#### Benchmarks.

We use the BFCL V3 multi-turn subset as the in-distribution benchmark
([Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)). It contains 800 examples from four
categories: Base, Missing Functions, Missing Parameters, and Long
Context. We focus on a *low-resource* setting with 400 training
examples, sampling 100 from each category, and use the remaining 400
examples for held-in evaluation. For *out-of-distribution* evaluation,
we use BFCL V4 Web Search and Memory, together with the Retail, Airline,
and Telecom domains of $`\tau^{2}`$-bench. These held-out benchmarks
differ from BFCL V3 in tool domains, schema structure, and interaction
patterns. Detailed protocols are provided in Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Benchmark and Evaluation Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments").

#### Models and baselines.

We evaluate SEAL on three backbones: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and ToolACE-2-Llama-3.1-8B. The Qwen models
represent general instruction-tuned agents, while ToolACE-2 provides a
stronger tool-specialized initialization. For each backbone, we compare
against Vanilla RL under the same training split, rollout budget,
optimizer family, and verifier reward, yielding a *controlled
comparison*. We also report representative open-source and proprietary
tool-use systems only as *reference points*, since they differ in scale
and training recipe and are therefore not controlled baselines.

#### Hyperparameters.

We use a GRPO-style optimizer with 8 rollouts per prompt. The actor
learning rate is set to $`1\times 10^{-6}`$, with a train batch size of
32, a PPO mini-batch size of 8, and a PPO micro-batch size of 1 per GPU.
We use a training temperature of 1.0 and a validation temperature of
0.0. The maximum prompt length, response length, and model length are
set to 8192, 4096, and 16384, respectively. Training is conducted with
vLLM-based asynchronous rollout workers on 4 GPUs. Additional
implementation details are provided in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments").

|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Model | BFCL V3 Multi-Turn |  |  |  |  |
|  | Average (%) | Base (%) | Miss Func (%) | Miss Param (%) | Long Context (%) |
| Closed-source |  |  |  |  |  |
| Gemini-3-Pro-Preview ([Google, 2025](#bib.bib56)) | 60.75 | 64.50 | 60.00 | 54.50 | 64.00 |
| Claude-Sonnet-4.5 ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib54)) | 61.38 | 69.00 | 65.00 | 52.50 | 59.00 |
| GPT-4o-2024-11-20 ([Hurst et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)) | 42.50 | 55.50 | 34.50 | 29.00 | 51.00 |

### 4.2 Main Results on BFCL V3

Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Hyperparameters. ‣ 4.1 Experiment Settings ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
reports in-distribution results on BFCL V3 multi-turn evaluation. We
compare each SEAL-trained model against its corresponding backbone and
Vanilla RL counterpart under the same 400-sample training budget.

Overall gains. SEAL improves all three backbones, increasing the average
score of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and
ToolACE-2-Llama-3.1-8B by +8.25, +26.25, and +14.75 points over their
original checkpoints. The gains are therefore consistent across model
scale and initialization quality, rather than being confined to a single
regime. Improvements on ToolACE-2-Llama-3.1-8B further show that the
method helps even a tool-specialized model.

Controlled comparison against Vanilla RL. Under the same training split,
rollout budget, optimizer family, and verifier reward, SEAL outperforms
Vanilla RL by +4.75, +9.50, and +8.25 average points across the three
backbones. This gap suggests that sparse terminal rewards alone are not
enough for efficient multi-turn tool-use learning. The advantage is
especially notable on the 7B and 8B models, indicating that the benefit
of verifier-grounded diagnosis remains substantial even when the
starting policy is already considerably stronger.

Where the gains are largest. The biggest improvements appear on
structured tool-use failures. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SEAL raises
Missing Functions from 14.00% to 36.00% and Missing Parameters from
10.00% to 34.00%, consistent with the error types the method is designed
to address. Gains on Long Context also suggest better multi-turn state
tracking and recovery. This pattern matters because these categories
capture failures that are common in practical tool use, where an agent
must choose the right tool, fill in the right arguments, and remain
consistent over multiple turns.

Taken together, these in-distribution results show that SEAL improves
not only final accuracy, but also the structured behaviors that matter
for reliable multi-turn tool use. A natural next question is whether
these gains transfer beyond BFCL V3.

### 4.3 Out-of-Distribution Generalization

Having established strong in-distribution gains, we next ask whether
they transfer to held-out tool-use settings with different task
distributions, tool domains, and interaction patterns. OOD transfer.
Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Out-of-Distribution Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
shows that SEAL improves both evaluated backbones and outperforms
Vanilla RL on the aggregate BFCL V4 and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench metrics. For
Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, it raises BFCL V4 from 4.69% to 8.63% and
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench from 9.64% to 11.76%. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, it
improves BFCL V4 from 9.17% to 12.71% and $`\tau^{2}`$-bench from 16.11%
to 20.79%.

$`\tau^{2}`$-bench. Models are trained only on the 400-sample BFCL V3

Interpretation. These results suggest that SEAL learns transferable
tool-use behaviors—such as argument grounding, error recovery, and
multi-turn state management—rather than simply fitting the 400 BFCL V3
training examples. At the same time, absolute OOD scores remain modest,
so cross-benchmark generalization is still challenging.

Taken together, the in-distribution and out-of-distribution results
point to a *mechanism-level* advantage: verifier-grounded diagnosis
improves both sample-efficient learning on BFCL V3 and transfer to
held-out settings. We therefore next ask which parts of the closed loop
matter most.

### 4.4 Ablation Study

To explain where the gains come from, we ablate the three mechanisms
built on verifier-grounded diagnosis: environment-side adaptation,
diagnosis-guided reweighting, and closed-loop interface updates. Since
diagnosis is the shared input to all SEAL components, removing it
entirely would reduce the method to Vanilla RL.

Relative contribution of each component. Removing diagnosis-guided
reweighting causes a larger drop than removing environment-side
adaptation, suggesting that diagnostic labels are especially important
for allocating policy-gradient pressure. Still, environment-side
adaptation contributes +4.50 points over the variant without it, and
Full SEAL outperforms both single-sided variants. This pattern suggests
that the two uses of diagnosis are complementary.

Together, these ablations show that SEAL’s advantage does not come from
a single ingredient, but from combining better training-time feedback
with better optimization of the resulting rollouts.

| Backbone and RL Baseline |  |  |  |  |  |

|    + Vanilla RL | 30.75 | 46.00 | 27.00 | 27.00 | 23.00 |

that environment-side adaptation, diagnosis-guided reweighting, and
closed-loop updates all contribute, with Full SEAL outperforming all
single-sided variants.

### 4.5 Training Dynamics

Having identified which components matter most, we finally examine *how*
the gains emerge during training. Learning dynamics. Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.5 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
compares the validation trajectories of Vanilla RL and SEAL across the
four BFCL V3 categories. SEAL improves more rapidly and reaches higher
validation accuracy on most subsets, especially on Missing Functions and
Missing Parameters, where failures often require identifying missing
tool use or repairing invalid arguments. On Base, both methods improve
early, but SEAL climbs faster and stabilizes at a higher level. The
contrast is larger on Missing Functions and Missing Parameters, where
Vanilla RL improves only gradually while SEAL opens a clearer gap as
training proceeds. Long Context remains the hardest subset for both
methods, but SEAL still shows a more consistent upward trend and a
higher final accuracy.

The overall curve is also smoother and higher for SEAL, suggesting that
the gains are not driven by a single subset but accumulate across
failure types over the course of training. The widening gap after the
early phase is consistent with SEAL’s closed-loop design: as the
policy’s dominant failures change, the training interface is updated to
expose more relevant cues, whereas Vanilla RL continues to receive the
same sparse terminal signal. This pattern supports the view that
verifier-grounded diagnosis not only improves final performance, but
also makes learning more targeted and sample-efficient throughout
training.

Figure 3: Training dynamics comparing Vanilla RL and SEAL on BFCL V3
validation subsets. We plot validation accuracy across training steps
for Base, Missing Functions, Missing Parameters, and Long Context.
Shaded regions denote binomial standard error estimated from each
100-sample validation subset.

## 5 Conclusion and Limitations

We introduced SEAL, a closed-loop framework for co-evolving tool-use
agents and their training-time learning environments. By using
verifier-grounded failure diagnosis as a shared signal for
learning-interface evolution and policy optimization, SEAL addresses
*Agent-Environment Misalignment* while preserving tool semantics, task
labels, and the evaluation verifier. Experiments on in-distribution and
out-of-distribution multi-turn tool-use benchmarks show consistent gains
in low-resource learning across multiple backbones.

More broadly, our results suggest that improving tool-use agents is not
only a matter of optimizing the policy against a fixed environment.
Adapting the training-time interface to the agent’s revealed failures
can make learning more targeted, sample-efficient, and robust to
structured multi-turn errors.

Several limitations remain. SEAL relies on executable environments with
tool schemas, execution traces, and verifier feedback, so more
open-ended domains may require richer diagnosis mechanisms and weaker
forms of supervision. Its environment evolution is intentionally
conservative, modifying the training-time interface rather than tool
semantics or evaluation rules, which preserves fairness but limits the
scope of adaptation. Diagnostic utility weights are also fixed across
tasks and backbones, and cross-domain generalization remains
challenging.

Future work includes extending diagnosis to less structured
environments, learning adaptive utility weights, and studying how
co-evolution scales to broader tool ecosystems and longer-horizon
agentic workflows.

## Appendix A Benchmark and Evaluation Details

#### BFCL V3.

Our in-distribution evaluation uses the multi-turn subset of the
Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) V3. The benchmark evaluates
whether an agent can correctly use executable tools over multi-turn
dialogue contexts. Each task contains a user instruction sequence, a set
of available tools, and an executable evaluation protocol. The subset
contains 800 examples across four categories: Base, Missing Functions,
Missing Parameters, and Long Context. Base evaluates standard multi-turn
function calling with complete tool information. Missing Functions tests
whether the agent can recognize when required tools are unavailable or
when no valid tool applies. Missing Parameters evaluates whether the
agent can handle underspecified arguments rather than hallucinating
missing values. Long Context stresses state tracking and tool-use
consistency over extended dialogue histories.

Following the low-resource setting in the main experiments, we construct
a 400-example training split by sampling 100 instances from each
category. The remaining 400 examples are used for held-in evaluation.
All SEAL and Vanilla RL runs use the same training split and held-in
test split, ensuring that performance differences are attributable to
the training method rather than data scale or split variation.

#### BFCL V4.

For out-of-distribution evaluation, we use the Web Search and Memory
tracks from BFCL V4. These tracks differ from BFCL V3 in tool schema
structure, task distribution, and interaction pattern. The Web Search
track evaluates whether an agent can retrieve and synthesize information
using search-style tools. The Memory track evaluates whether an agent
can store, retrieve, and update memory-like information across
interactions. Since SEAL is trained only on the BFCL V3 training split,
BFCL V4 serves as a held-out benchmark for testing cross-distribution
transfer.

#### $`\tau^{2}`$-bench.

We also evaluate on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench across the Retail, Airline, and
Telecom domains. These tasks require multi-turn tool use in simulated
customer-service environments, where the agent must follow domain
policies, interact with tools, and maintain task state across turns.
Compared with BFCL, $`\tau^{2}`$-bench introduces different tool
semantics, domain constraints, and user-agent interaction patterns,
making it a complementary testbed for OOD generalization.

#### Evaluation protocol and metric.

All evaluations are performed using the original benchmark environments
and verifiers. SEAL-specific diagnostic feedback, interface
augmentation, capability-specific hints, and recovery-oriented training
messages are disabled during evaluation. Thus, all reported results
measure the policy under the original test-time protocol. We report
success rate as the primary metric:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{SR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\left[\mathcal{V}(\tau_{q},q,\mathcal{E})=1\right],
``` |  | (17) |

where $`\mathcal{Q}`$ is the evaluation set and $`\tau_{q}`$ is the
trajectory generated for instruction $`q`$. Category-level scores are
computed on the corresponding subset, and average scores are computed as
the arithmetic mean over reported categories.

## Appendix B SEAL Training Algorithm

Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix B SEAL Training Algorithm ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
summarizes the full SEAL training procedure. SEAL alternates between
policy rollout, verifier-grounded diagnosis, diagnosis-guided interface
evolution, and policy optimization. The interface wrapper is used only
during training and is removed during final evaluation.

1: Initial policy $`\pi_{\theta_{0}}`$, reference policy
$`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$, training prompts $`\mathcal{D}`$, base
environment $`\mathcal{E}`$, verifier $`\mathcal{V}`$, number of rounds
$`R`$, rollouts per prompt $`G`$

2: Initial interface wrapper $`\Omega_{0}`$, diagnostic utility
$`\rho(z)`$, clipping range $`[w_{\min},w_{\max}]`$

3: for $`r=0,1,\ldots,R-1`$ do

4:   Sample prompt batch $`\mathcal{X}_{r}\subset\mathcal{D}`$

5:   Construct training environment
$`\mathcal{E}_{\Omega_{r}}\leftarrow\Omega_{r}(\mathcal{E})`$

6:   Initialize rollout buffer $`\mathcal{R}_{r}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

7:   for each prompt $`x\in\mathcal{X}_{r}`$ do

8:    Sample $`G`$ trajectories $`\{\tau_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$ from
$`\pi_{\theta_{r}}`$ in $`\mathcal{E}_{\Omega_{r}}`$

9:    for each trajectory $`\tau_{j}`$ do

10:      Compute verifier reward
$`r_{j}\leftarrow\mathcal{V}(\tau_{j},x,\mathcal{E})`$

11:      Diagnose trajectory
$`Z(\tau_{j})\leftarrow\Psi(\tau_{j},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{V})`$

12:      Store $`(x,\tau_{j},r_{j},Z(\tau_{j}))`$ in $`\mathcal{R}_{r}`$

13:    end for

14:   end for

15:   Aggregate failure profile
$`C_{r}\leftarrow\operatorname{Agg}(\{Z(\tau_{j}):\tau_{j}\in\mathcal{R}_{r}\})`$

16:   for each prompt group in $`\mathcal{R}_{r}`$ do

17:    Compute group-relative advantages $`A_{j}`$ from verifier rewards
$`\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$

18:    Compute diagnostic weights
$`w_{j}\leftarrow\operatorname{clip}(\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{\tau_{j}}(z)\rho(z),w_{\min},w_{\max})`$

19:    Set weighted advantages
$`\widetilde{A}_{j}\leftarrow w_{j}A_{j}`$

20:   end for

21:   Update policy $`\pi_{\theta_{r}}\rightarrow\pi_{\theta_{r+1}}`$
using GRPO with $`\widetilde{A}_{j}`$ and KL regularization

22:   Update interface $`\Omega_{r+1}\leftarrow U(\Omega_{r},C_{r})`$

23: end for

24: return trained policy $`\pi_{\theta_{R}}`$

Algorithm 1 SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning
Environments

At evaluation time, SEAL discards the training-time interface wrapper
and evaluates $`\pi_{\theta_{R}}`$ in the original environment
$`\mathcal{E}`$ with the unchanged verifier $`\mathcal{V}`$.

## Appendix C Experimental Details

This section provides implementation details for reproducing the
training runs and for verifying that SEAL is compared against Vanilla RL
under a controlled protocol. Unless otherwise stated, all BFCL
experiments use the same base model, training split, rollout budget,
decoding configuration, and evaluation verifier across methods.

### C.1 Hyperparameter Configuration

Table
[4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.1 Hyperparameter Configuration ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments")
summarizes the main training configuration used in our BFCL experiments.
We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the default backbone for the main BFCL
experiments and apply the same GRPO configuration to Vanilla RL and
SEAL. The only algorithmic differences are whether verifier-grounded
diagnosis, diagnosis-guided interface evolution, closed-loop
failure-profile updates, and diagnostic advantage weighting are enabled.

|                     |                            |                     |
|---------------------|----------------------------|---------------------|
| Category            | Hyperparameter             | Value               |
| Policy optimization | Base model                 | Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct |
|                     | Training method            | GRPO                |
|                     | Actor learning rate        | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ |
|                     | Train batch size           | 32                  |
|                     | PPO mini-batch size        | 8                   |
|                     | PPO micro-batch size / GPU | 1                   |
| Rollout             | Inference engine           | vLLM (async)        |
|                     | Rollouts per prompt        | 8                   |
|                     | Training temperature       | 1.0                 |
|                     | Validation temperature     | 0.0                 |
|                     | Max prompt length          | 8192                |
|                     | Max response length        | 4096                |
|                     | Max model length           | 16384               |
| Multi-turn setting  | Number of training samples | 400                 |
|                     | Multi-turn rollout         | Enabled             |
|                     | Max interaction steps      | 20                  |
|                     | Tool format                | llama3_json         |
|                     | BFCL tool prompt mode      | bfcl_qwen_fc        |
| Regularization      | Reward KL penalty          | Disabled            |
|                     | Actor KL loss coefficient  | 0.001               |
|                     | Entropy coefficient        | 0.0                 |
| Hardware            | GPUs                       | 4                   |
|                     | Tensor parallel size       | 1                   |
|                     | GPU memory utilization     | 0.6                 |
|                     | Max environment workers    | 32                  |

Table 4: Main hyperparameter configuration for BFCL experiments. Unless
otherwise specified, Vanilla RL and SEAL use the same optimization,
rollout, and evaluation settings.

For ablations with different backbones, we keep the same data split,
rollout budget, verifier, decoding configuration, and evaluation
protocol whenever possible. When hardware constraints require changes to
micro-batch size or gradient accumulation, we keep the effective batch
size fixed.

### C.2 Diagnosis Label Priority

When multiple failures are detected at the same turn, SEAL assigns the
dominant label according to a fixed priority order. The priority favors
directly executable failures over downstream verifier-level failures, as
shown in Table
[5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ C.2 Diagnosis Label Priority ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ SEAL: Synergistic Co-Evolution of Agents and Learning Environments").

| Priority | Label |  Rationale |
|----|----|----|
| 1 | invalid_tool_call |  The action is not parseable or calls an unavailable tool. |
| 2 | argument_mismatch |  The tool is valid, but required fields, types, enum values, or argument structure are invalid. |
| 3 | state_mismatch |  The action executes but fails to produce the expected observable state transition. |
| 4 | recovery_failure |  The model receives executable error feedback but fails to recover in later turns. |
| 5 | missing_tool_call |  The trajectory fails because the model skips necessary tool use or responds prematurely. |
| 6 | response_mismatch |  Tool interaction is acceptable, but the final answer fails the verifier. |

Table 5: Priority order for assigning diagnostic labels when multiple
failure signals are present.

This priority prevents SEAL from attributing a trajectory-level failure
to a generic response mismatch when a concrete tool or argument error is
already observed. For example, if a trajectory fails the final verifier
because an earlier tool call used an invalid argument, SEAL assigns
argument_mismatch rather than response_mismatch.

| Diagnostic Label | $`\rho(z)`$ | Rationale |
|----|----|----|
| spurious_tool_call | 2.0 | Invalid or unnecessary tool use is directly attributable. |
| correct_abstention | 1.8 | Rewards learning when no tool should be called. |
| empty_turn_model_response | 1.5 | Captures missed tool-use or premature non-action. |
| state_mismatch | 1.0 | Indicates failure to reach the expected environment state. |
| response_mismatch | 0.9 | Final response is wrong, but attribution is less localized. |
| instance_mismatch | 0.6 | Instance errors are useful but often noisier or less localized. |
| pass | 1.0 | Successful trajectories keep the baseline update scale. |

Table 6: Diagnostic utility weights used by SEAL.

We clip the resulting trajectory-level diagnostic weight to
$`[w_{\min},w_{\max}]=[0.5,2.0]`$ to avoid overly large updates from
rare or noisy diagnostic patterns.

### C.3 Controlled Comparison Protocol

The comparison between Vanilla RL and SEAL is controlled along the
following dimensions. Both methods use the same initial checkpoint, the
same set of 400 BFCL V3 training samples, the same number of rollouts
per prompt, the same optimizer, and the same decoding configuration.
Both methods are evaluated using the original BFCL V3 multi-turn
environment and the official verifier.

Vanilla RL optimizes the standard GRPO objective using only verifier
rewards. SEAL uses the same verifier rewards and the same GRPO backbone,
but additionally uses verifier-grounded diagnoses from training rollouts
to construct training-time interface updates and diagnostic utility
weights. No method receives ground-truth tool trajectories, hidden
parameter values, reference intermediate actions, or final answers
during training.

The evolved SEAL interface is used only during training. During
evaluation, the wrapper is removed, and the model interacts with the
original benchmark interface. Thus, SEAL and Vanilla RL are evaluated
under identical test-time conditions. The comparison therefore measures
whether the policy has internalized better tool-use behavior, rather
than whether it has access to additional test-time information.

### C.4 Logging and Reproducibility

For each run, we log the random seed, base checkpoint, code version,
training configuration, configuration overrides, rollout budget,
decoding parameters, validation scores, round-level failure profiles
$`C_{r}`$, interface states $`\Omega_{r}`$, diagnostic label
distributions, and final evaluation outputs. These logs allow us to
verify that changes in performance are attributable to SEAL components
rather than differences in training budget, data split, decoding
configuration, or evaluation protocol.

## Appendix D Prompt and Interface Templates

This section reports the prompt and training-time interface templates
used in our BFCL implementation. The base tool-use prompt is shared by
Vanilla RL and SEAL. SEAL modifies only the training-time environment
interface, for example by annotating tool schemas, enriching failed tool
feedback when enabled, or injecting short behavioral guidelines derived
from recent diagnostic profiles. All SEAL-specific interface
augmentations are disabled during evaluation.

### D.1 Base BFCL Tool-Use Prompt

For Qwen-style BFCL experiments, the environment serializes the
available tools into the system prompt using the following template.
This base prompt is used by both Vanilla RL and SEAL.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The base prompt defines the tool-call format and exposes the available
tool schemas. It does not contain SEAL-specific diagnostic labels,
recovery hints, or capability-dependent instructions.

### D.2 Schema Observation Annotation

In our active BFCL configuration, SEAL uses a lightweight observation
annotation mechanism. When observation_lite is enabled, SEAL does not
change tool APIs, tool signatures, tool outputs, or verifier behavior.
Instead, it augments the exposed schema descriptions with lightweight
annotations that make existing constraints more explicit.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The environment also appends the following training-time instruction:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This annotation corresponds to the schema-affordance component
$`\phi_{\mathrm{schema}}`$. It exposes only public schema information,
such as required arguments and enum constraints, and does not reveal the
correct tool choice, hidden parameter values, reference tool trajectory,
or final answer for any instance.

### D.3 Tool Feedback Evolution Template

When tool_feedback_evolution is enabled, SEAL enriches only failed
interactions. This component corresponds to the recovery-feedback
component $`\phi_{\mathrm{err}}`$. It converts low-level parse or
execution errors into structured recovery hints, while preserving the
original tool API and verifier.

For parser failures, the environment may append format-specific hints
such as:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For execution errors, the environment may append tool-specific but
non-solution-revealing hints such as:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These hints identify the class of tool-use error and the violated
interface constraint. They do not provide the next correct tool call,
instance-specific argument values, or the ground-truth solution
trajectory.

### D.4 Diagnostic Evolution Guideline Template

When diagnostic_evolution is enabled, SEAL reads recent failure
statistics from the capability profile and injects short behavioral
guidelines into the system prompt. This component corresponds to
$`\phi_{\mathrm{cap}}`$: the interface is adjusted according to
recurring failure modes of the current policy rather than individual
benchmark instances.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The guidelines are selected from aggregate failure patterns, such as
spurious tool calls, missing tool calls, state mismatches, or
final-response format errors. They are capability-level instructions
rather than per-instance hints. Therefore, they do not expose the
reference trajectory, hidden state, hidden argument values, or target
answer of any benchmark example.

#### Active configuration.

In the BFCL configuration used for the main rerun, the active
training-time interface uses the base BFCL prompt together with
observation_lite schema annotation. The additional
tool_feedback_evolution and diagnostic_evolution templates are included
here to document the complete SEAL interface implementation, and should
be interpreted as optional components when enabled by configuration.

## Appendix E Qualitative Case Studies

We present four qualitative case studies to illustrate how SEAL improves
multi-turn tool use across different capability types: file-system state
tracking, API-parameter recovery, cross-domain tool composition, and
vehicle-control state maintenance. Each case compares the behavior of
the base model before SEAL training with the behavior of the
SEAL-trained model on the same BFCL task. We also include the expected
outcome for post-hoc analysis only; these references are not exposed to
the policy during training or evaluation.

We focus on critical turns where the base model fails and the
SEAL-trained model succeeds. These examples are not intended to replace
the controlled Vanilla RL comparison in the main experiments; rather,
they illustrate the types of tool-use failures that SEAL is designed to
diagnose and correct.

### E.1 File-System State Tracking

This case studies a file-system task requiring the agent to compare
report files, move and rename a note file inside an archive directory,
retrieve a support ticket, and finally resolve it. The key challenge is
maintaining the current directory state and respecting file-system tool
constraints.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Failure analysis. The base model locates the relevant file names only
after an initial failure, but continues to issue invalid path-style
arguments to mv. This indicates that it does not convert the execution
error into a revised state-aware plan.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Success analysis. The SEAL-trained model uses observable directory
contents to infer the actual file names, then respects the
local-directory constraint by moving into archives before renaming the
file. This shows improved recovery from tool feedback and better
file-system state tracking.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Recovering from API Parameter Mismatch

This case studies a travel API task. The user asks for the economy
flight cost from Rivermist to Stonebrook on October 6, 2026, and later
asks to set a spending budget provided in GBP. The model must recover
from invalid airport parameters and convert the budget into the expected
currency.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Failure analysis. The base model treats guessed airport codes as final
and does not use the airport-resolution tools after the route error. It
also sets the GBP amount directly as the budget limit, missing the
required currency conversion.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Success analysis. The SEAL-trained model recovers by using the missing
airport-resolution tools and later converts GBP to USD before calling
set_budget_limit. This reflects better handling of intermediate API
dependencies and parameter constraints.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Cross-Domain Tool Composition

This case combines stock-market and Twitter APIs. The model must
retrieve the price of Omega Industries, insert the price into a tweet,
include \#TechBoom and @industryexperts, and later add @technewsworld to
the existing tweet.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Failure analysis. The base model substitutes Apple for Omega Industries
after the guessed symbol fails, thereby changing the user’s target
entity. It also posts a new tweet rather than adding the new mention to
the existing tweet.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Success analysis. The SEAL-trained model treats the failed symbol lookup
as recoverable evidence, resolves the company name to OMEG, retrieves
the correct price, and updates the existing tweet with the dedicated
mention tool.

### E.4 Vehicle-Control State Maintenance

This case studies long-context vehicle control. The user first fills the
car with 13.2 gallons, asks the agent to fill the tank to its maximum
limit, lock the doors, and set the parking brake. Later, the user asks
the agent to start the engine and check the fuel level before posting a
road-trip tweet.

Failure analysis. The base model verbally computes the remaining
capacity but never executes fillFuelTank. The later engine check
therefore reports fuelLevel = 13.2, revealing that the required state
update did not occur.

Note (Failure Point): The baseline resolves only one issue: data
````
